title: Gifts from Above
sum: James opens with a one-line greeting to "the twelve tribes in the Dispersion" and goes straight to hardship. Trials are to be counted as joy, because faith that is proved produces endurance, and endurance makes a person complete (1:2-4). Whoever lacks wisdom should ask God, who gives freely, but must ask without a divided heart (1:5-8). The poor brother is lifted up and the rich man will wither like a wildflower (1:9-11).

Testing is not temptation: God tempts no one, and sin is born of a person's own desire (1:12-15). Every good gift comes from the unchanging Father of the lights, who gave believers new birth by the word of truth (1:16-18). That word must be received and done, not only heard. The one who looks into the complete law of freedom and acts is blessed; true religion cares for orphans and widows and stays clean of the world (1:19-27).
readings: A string of sayings

Many readers see chapter 1 as a collection of short wisdom sayings, linked by catchwords: "short of nothing" (1:4) and "short of wisdom" (1:5), "trial" and "tempt" (1:12-13), "word" (1:18-23). On this reading James is a teacher of wisdom, like the writer of Proverbs or Sirach, and the chapter is an overture that names the themes the rest of the letter develops: trials, wisdom, rich and poor, speech, anger, and doing the word.
A sermon with a plan

Others find a planned argument: God is the giver of good (1:5, 17), people are the source of their own temptation (1:13-15), and the gift God gives is the word that gives birth (1:18) and must be done (1:22-25). Read this way, the chapter sets God's single-minded giving against the double-minded person, and the rest of the letter applies the contrast.

views.H: The readers are scattered communities under pressure: poor (1:9; 2:5), dragged into court by the rich (2:6), at risk of anger and quarrels (1:19-20; 4:1). "Trials" are the hardships of poor believers in a world run by wealthy landowners and merchants.
views.C: Critical readers note how little in the chapter is distinctly Christian: "the Lord Jesus Christ" (1:1) and perhaps the new birth by the word (1:18). Luther already complained in 1522 that the letter "does not once mention the Passion, the resurrection, or the Spirit of Christ". The good Greek of the chapter (including a line that scans as verse, 1:17) is one argument in the authorship debate.
views.L: Chain links bind the chapter: rejoice/joy (1:1-2), endurance/endurance (1:3-4), short of/short of (1:4-5), ask/ask (1:5-6), trial/tempt (1:12-13), desire conceives/he brought us to birth (1:15, 18), hearer/doer (1:22-25), religious/religion (1:26-27).
views.J: The chapter breathes Jewish wisdom: wisdom asked of God (Proverbs 2:6; Wisdom of Solomon 9), the warning not to blame God for one's fall (Sirach 15:11-20), the inclination to evil within (Genesis 8:21), the Torah as a law that gives life and freedom (Psalm 19:7), and care for orphans and widows (Deuteronomy 10:18).
views.T: The Lutheran Apology of the Augsburg Confession read 1:18 as proof that James teaches new birth through the gospel, not by works. Luther's 1522 preface set the "law of liberty" (1:25) against Paul's teaching on the law. 1:17 is often quoted for God's unchanging goodness, and 1:27 for the church's care of orphans and widows.

deep.b:
English Bibles divide one Greek family of words into two: "trial" (1:2, 12) and "tempt" (1:13-14). James uses the overlap to make a point. The same event, poverty, illness, injustice, can be a trial that proves faith and builds endurance, or a temptation that drags a person into sin. Which it becomes depends on the person's response, not on God. God "put Abraham to the test" (Genesis 22:1), but God never baits anyone toward evil (1:13).

James traces temptation to "his own desire" (1:14). He does not mention the devil here, though he will in 4:7. Jewish wisdom had the same emphasis: "Do not say, 'It was because of the Lord that I fell away'" (Sirach 15:11), and the rabbis spoke of the evil inclination (yetzer hara) in every heart, a word drawn from Genesis 8:21: "what the human heart shapes is evil from youth on."

Chapter 1 has two family trees. In the first, desire becomes pregnant, gives birth to sin, and sin grows up and bears death (1:15). In the second, God by his own will brings us to birth by the word of truth, to be the firstfruits of his creation (1:18). James uses the same rare verb (apokyeo) for both births. The contrast is the letter's whole theology in small: human desire produces death; God's word produces new life, and that word, once planted (1:21), has to be done (1:22).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the mirror and the face of Genesis
deep.b: In 1:23 James says the forgetful hearer looks at the face he was born with; the Greek is literally the face of his genesis. The word genesis returns in 3:6, "the wheel of genesis". It is possible that James chose the word to hint at Genesis 1:26: the hearer who looks into the law should see the face God made, the likeness of God (which James names in 3:9), and live up to it. The forgetful hearer walks away and forgets "what kind of man he was", that is, forgets that he bears God's image. This is my own suggestion. The KJV renders the phrase "his natural face", and genesis here may mean no more than "the face he was born with", as the Plain has it.

echoes: Matthew 5:11-12; Matthew 7:7; Matthew 7:24-27; Romans 5:3-5; 1 Peter 1:6-7; 1 Peter 1:23-24; Isaiah 40:6-8; Sirach 15:11-20; Genesis 1:14-18; Deuteronomy 10:18

settings.by: James, "a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ"
settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: Not stated. If James the Lord's brother wrote it, from Jerusalem before about AD 62; if not, later
settings.why: To present the writer by his name alone, as a servant, and to claim the readers as Israel's twelve tribes living away from home. The form is a Jewish "Dispersion letter", like the letters Jerusalem leaders sent to Jews abroad, and like the letter of Acts 15:23, which opens with the same word, "greetings".
views: The twelve tribes are Jewish Christians outside the land, addressed by the head of the Jerusalem church.
The twelve tribes are all believers, Jewish and Gentile, seen as the renewed Israel scattered in the world (compare 1 Peter 1:1).
Written by James the Lord's brother before his death (about AD 62), perhaps in the 40s before the council of Acts 15, or in the 50s. It would then be one of the earliest Christian writings.
Written in James' name late in the first century or early in the second, for churches that honored him, perhaps in answer to a misuse of Paul's teaching.

settings.what: Trials, wisdom, rich and poor, and the giver of good gifts
settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: To communities living with poverty and pressure from the rich (1:9-11; 2:6-7)
settings.why: To teach the readers to see their hardships as a test that builds endurance, to ask God for the wisdom to bear them, to stop blaming God when hardship becomes temptation, and to remember that God gives only good. Knowing the readers were mostly poor explains why the rich man's fall and the lowly brother's rise come right after the call to joy in trials.

settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: To believers who heard Scripture and teaching read aloud in their meetings
settings.why: To make sure that hearing becomes doing. In a community that met every week to hear the law and the word, the danger was hearing without change. James defines true religion by its deeds: control of the tongue, care for orphans and widows, and a life unstained by the world.

title: Faith That Works
sum: James turns to the church's meeting. When a man with gold rings is given a good seat and a poor man is told to stand or sit on the floor, the church has judged by appearances and dishonored those God chose to be rich in faith (2:1-7). Favoritism breaks the royal law, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself", and one who breaks one command has broken the law that one God gave (2:8-11). Speak and act as people who will be judged by the law of freedom: mercy triumphs over judgment (2:12-13).

Then comes the most debated passage in the letter. Faith that says "Go in peace" to a hungry brother and gives nothing is dead (2:14-17). Belief that God is one is good, but the demons believe that too (2:18-19). Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and so the Scripture "Abraham believed God" came true; Rahab too was justified by works (2:20-25). "It is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (2:24). As a body without breath is dead, so is faith without works (2:26).
readings: James against Paul

Some readers, Luther among them in 1522, have found James in direct conflict with Paul: Paul says "a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28) and uses Abraham to prove it (Romans 4); James says the opposite and uses Abraham too. On this reading one must choose, or rank one above the other.
James and Paul answering different questions

Most readers in every church have read the two as complementary. Paul asks how a sinner is first accepted by God, and answers: by faith, not by keeping the Torah. James asks what kind of faith is real, and answers: faith that acts. The words differ in meaning: James' "faith" is belief the demons share; his "works" are acts of mercy; his "justified" may mean shown or judged righteous. Some think James was answering people who had twisted Paul's teaching (as Wesley's notes say), others that he wrote before Paul's letters and knew nothing of them.
A Jewish reading

Read within Judaism, James says nothing surprising: faith in the one God (2:19) is lived out in obedience, Abraham was proved faithful in his test (1 Maccabees 2:52), and mercy to the poor is central to the law. Read this way, the tension with Paul becomes a debate inside early Jewish Christianity about how Gentiles share in Abraham's family.

views.H: Seating in the meeting showed rank, as at any ancient banquet or gathering. A gold-ringed visitor would be a patron the church might hope to win. James' readers were themselves dragged into court by such people (2:6).
views.C: Whether James knew Paul's letters, or a slogan drawn from them ("faith alone"), is the key question for dating the letter. Those who date it early see no contact; those who date it late see James answering a misuse of Paul. The phrase "not by faith alone" (2:24) seems to answer someone who said "by faith alone", but Paul's surviving letters never use that phrase.
views.L: The diatribe style is clear: questions (2:4-7, 14, 20-21, 25), an imagined objector (2:18), a scolding "You empty man" (2:20). The argument has three examples (the hungry brother, the demons, Abraham and Rahab) and a closing comparison (2:26).
views.J: The chapter rests on Leviticus 19 (no favoritism, 19:15; love your neighbor, 19:18), the Ten Commandments, the Shema (2:19), and the Jewish tradition that counted the binding of Isaac as Abraham's great test (1 Maccabees 2:52; Sirach 44:20). The "synagogue" (2:2) suggests a Jewish-Christian community.
views.T: 2:24 has been at the center of the debate between the churches on justification since the Reformation. See the card below, and the deep dive on James and Paul.

deep.h: James and Paul, side by side
deep.b:
The two writers use the same words and the same Abraham:

Paul: "For we reckon that a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28). "If Abraham was justified by works, he has a reason to boast, though not with God" (Romans 4:2). "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Romans 4:3).

James: "So you see that it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (2:24). "Take Abraham our father. When he laid his son Isaac on the altar as an offering, was he not justified by works?" (2:21).

Four differences matter. (1) Faith: for James, the faith in question is a belief that can be held without obedience ("the demons believe it as well", 2:19); for Paul, faith is trust that joins a person to Christ and "works through love" (Galatians 5:6). (2) Works: James means acts of mercy and obedience (2:15-16, 21, 25); Paul's "works of the law" are the deeds the Torah required, often those that marked Jews off from Gentiles. (3) Abraham: Paul points to Genesis 15:6, before Abraham was circumcised; James to Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac, which he calls the fulfillment of 15:6. (4) Justify: Paul means God's acceptance of the ungodly; James may mean the final verdict, or the showing of righteousness.

The 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, signed by the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church, lists James 2:14-26 among the New Testament's "diverse treatments" of righteousness and justification (paragraph 9), and the two churches confess together that good works "follow justification and are its fruits" (paragraph 37). The World Methodist Council affirmed the declaration in 2006, the Anglican Consultative Council "welcomed and affirmed the substance" of it in 2016, and the World Communion of Reformed Churches later associated itself with it.

James did not invent his reading of Abraham. Before him, 1 Maccabees joined the binding of Isaac to the words of Genesis 15:6: "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" (1 Maccabees 2:52). Sirach 44:20 says that he kept the law of the Most High and "in testing he was found faithful". In this tradition Abraham's faith and his obedience are one story, completed on Mount Moriah. James stands in it; Paul, writing to Gentiles who were being told to become Jews, reads the same Abraham from the other end, before circumcision and before the law.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the hungry brother and Abraham's tent
deep.b: James' two models of faith that works are Abraham and Rahab, and in Scripture's own telling both welcomed strangers: Abraham ran to feed three strangers (Genesis 18:1-8), and Rahab took in the messengers (Joshua 2; 2:25). James' opening example of dead faith is a failure of the same virtue: a brother or sister without clothes or food sent away with "Go in peace" (2:15-16). It may be that James chose his examples so that the whole passage turns on welcoming the needy, the very thing the church failed to do for the poor man in 2:2-4. This is my own reading. A simpler explanation is that James chose a famous patriarch and a famous outsider.

echoes: Leviticus 19:15; Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 6:4; Genesis 15:6; Genesis 22:1-18; Joshua 2:1-21; Romans 3:28; Romans 4:1-5; Galatians 2:16; Galatians 5:6; Matthew 5:3; Matthew 5:7; Luke 6:20; 1 Maccabees 2:52; Hebrews 11:17-19; Hebrews 11:31

settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: Written to communities where wealthy visitors were welcomed with honor while poor members were pushed aside, and where the rich outside the church oppressed the members (2:6-7)
settings.why: To shame the church out of copying the world's rank. Knowing that the readers were mostly poor and harmed by the rich makes the scene sharper: they were flattering the very people who dragged them into court. James grounds his command in the law itself (Leviticus 19:15, 18) and in the final judgment.
views: The assembly is gathered for prayer and teaching, and the seats show status.

Roy Bowen Ward (1969) argued that the assembly is the church sitting as a court to settle a dispute, which explains "judges" (2:4) and the courts of 2:6. The IVP New Testament Commentary finds this "intriguing but not conclusive".

settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: Written to believers some of whom claimed faith as enough while neglecting the poor
settings.why: To show that faith which does nothing is not saving faith at all. For readers who said "Go in peace" to the hungry, the point was practical before it was doctrinal: real faith clothes and feeds. Knowing the setting (a poor community, a quarrel over rank) keeps the passage from being read only as a debate about the order of salvation.
views: James corrects people who took Paul's "by faith, apart from works of the law" as permission to ignore obedience. Wesley's notes read it this way.
James writes early, or without knowledge of Paul's letters, against a lazy faith common in any church; the likeness of wording is due to shared Jewish language about Abraham.
James (or a later writer in his name) deliberately rejects Paul's teaching, as Luther believed in 1522.

traditions.q: James says "it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (2:24). How does this fit with justification by faith?
views: The Council of Trent quotes this verse to teach that the justified "increase in that justice which they have received", "faith co-operating with good works" (session 6, chapter 10). Faith without hope and charity does not unite a person perfectly with Christ (chapter 7), and Trent condemned the teaching that "by faith alone the impious is justified" without any movement of the will (canon 9). The Catechism adds that "no one can merit the initial grace of forgiveness and justification" (2010) and that justification "establishes cooperation between God's grace and man's freedom" (1993).

The Confession of Dositheus, a seventeenth-century confession adopted by a regional council (the Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), teaches that a person is "not simply justified through faith alone, but through faith which works through love, that is to say, through faith and works" (Decree 13). It rejects the idea that faith is a hand that lays hold of Christ's righteousness, and calls works "fruits" through which faith becomes effective.

The Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531) answers that James "does not contradict us": he condemns a dead faith and speaks of the works that follow a living faith; "to be justified" here means to be "pronounced righteous", as those who have faith and good works are. The Formula of Concord also rejects "a dead faith ... without repentance and without good works" (Solid Declaration, article 4). Luther himself, in his 1522 preface, judged James "flatly against St. Paul" on this point and would not count it among the chief books, though he kept it in his Bible.

Faith is "the alone instrument of justification; yet is it not alone in the person justified ... it is no dead faith, but worketh by love" (Westminster Confession 11.2). Calvin held that James "is speaking of the manifestation, not of the imputation of righteousness": his aim is "to destroy the depraved security of those who vainly pretended faith" (Institutes 3.17.11-12).

"That we are justified by Faith only is a most wholesome Doctrine" (Article 11), yet good works "do spring out necessarily of a true and lively Faith; insomuch that by them a lively Faith may be as evidently known as a tree discerned by the fruit" (Article 12).

John Wesley taught that the two apostles speak of two justifications: Abraham was "accounted righteous" by faith before his works (Paul's sense), and "made righteous" by works after his faith (James' sense), so that "St. James's justification by works is the fruit of St Paul's justification by faith". James refutes "not the doctrine of St. Paul, but the error of those who abused it" (Explanatory Notes on James 2). The World Methodist Council affirmed the Lutheran-Catholic Joint Declaration in 2006.

Justification is "God's gracious and full acquittal ... of all sinners who repent and believe in Christ", and sanctification, which begins in regeneration, follows (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 4). The article says that "repentance and faith are inseparable experiences of grace", and it lists James 2:14-26 among its supporting texts beside Romans 3-6, without explaining how the two fit together.

title: The Tongue and the Wisdom from Above
sum: James warns that not many should become teachers, since those who use words will be judged by them (3:1-2). The tongue is small but powerful, like the bit in a horse's mouth, the rudder of a ship, or the spark that burns a forest. It is a fire, a world of injustice, lit from Gehenna, and no human can tame it (3:3-8). With the same mouth people bless God and curse those made in his likeness, though no spring gives sweet and bitter water together (3:9-12).

True wisdom shows itself in a good life lived with gentleness (3:13). Bitter jealousy and rivalry are a "wisdom" that is earthly, merely natural and demonic, and they produce chaos (3:14-16). The wisdom from above is clean, peaceable, fair-minded, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, without hypocrisy, and its harvest is righteousness sown in peace by peacemakers (3:17-18).
readings: A warning to teachers

Read with 3:1, the whole chapter is about teachers: those who speak in the assembly must master their tongues (3:2-12) and show true wisdom rather than rivalry (3:13-18). The "wise and understanding" of 3:13 are the would-be teachers.
A general teaching on speech

Read with 1:19 and 1:26, the chapter widens to every believer: James is developing his command to be "slow to talk", with images drawn from the common stock of moral teaching, and then contrasts two kinds of wisdom as two ways of life.

views.H: In a small community that met to hear teaching, gossip, rivalry between teachers and harsh words could split the church. The images (horses, ships, forest fires, springs, figs and olives) are drawn from daily life around the Mediterranean and in the land of Israel.
views.C: The polished Greek of this chapter, with its chains of images and a rare phrase like "the wheel of existence" (3:6), is one of the main arguments of those who doubt that a Galilean like James wrote the letter. Others answer that Galilee was open to Greek culture, or that James used a skilled helper.
views.L: The chapter moves in pairs: small and great (3:3-5), blessing and curse (3:9-10), sweet and bitter (3:11), fig and olive, vine and fig (3:12), wisdom from below and from above (3:15-17). The list of wisdom's virtues in 3:17 is built with sound: eirenike, epieikes, eupeithes.
views.J: Jewish wisdom is full of warnings about speech (Proverbs 18:21; Psalm 39:1; Sirach 28:12). Cursing a person made in God's image (Genesis 1:26; 9:6) is an attack on God. "Wise and understanding" is Deuteronomy's phrase for a people who keep God's rules (Deuteronomy 4:6).
views.T: 3:1 has been read as a warning to all who teach in the church; 3:6, "Gehenna sets it on fire", has been read of the devil's work through speech (the Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary: "that is, of the devil"). The list in 3:17 has been used in Christian teaching on discernment, beside Paul's fruit of the Spirit.

deep.b:
James sets out two kinds of wisdom in a way close to the Jewish teaching of "the two ways" (Deuteronomy 30:15-20; Psalm 1). One comes "from above" (3:15, 17), the same place every good gift comes from (1:17), and it is given to anyone who asks God without doubting (1:5). The other is earthly, belongs to the merely natural self, and is demonic (3:15). Each is known by what it produces: the false wisdom by jealousy, rivalry, chaos and "every vile practice" (3:16); the true wisdom by peace, mercy and good fruit (3:17-18).

Wisdom for James is not cleverness but a way of life ("let his good life show his works", 3:13). In this he is closer to Proverbs than to the Greek philosophers: the wise person is the one who lives rightly.

echoes: Proverbs 18:21; Psalm 39:1; Psalm 140:3; Genesis 1:26; Genesis 9:6; Matthew 5:9; Matthew 5:22; Matthew 7:16; Matthew 12:34-37; Sirach 28:12; Galatians 5:20-23; Deuteronomy 4:6

settings.by: James, who counts himself a teacher ("we", 3:1)
settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: To churches where many wanted to teach and where quarrels were breaking out (3:14-16; 4:1-2)
settings.why: To cool the eagerness to teach and to warn every speaker that words carry judgment. For a scattered, pressured community, the tongue was the quickest way to tear itself apart. The images make the warning memorable.

settings.what: Wisdom from above and from below
settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: Where would-be teachers competed with jealousy and rivalry
settings.why: To give the community a test for true wisdom: not eloquence or knowledge but gentleness, peace and mercy. Knowing that rival teachers were causing division explains why "peace" is the last word of the chapter, just before "wars" opens chapter 4.

title: Friends of God, or of the World
sum: The wars and fights among the readers come from the pleasures at war inside them: they want, envy, fight, and still do not have, because they do not ask, or ask only for their pleasures (4:1-3). Friendship with the world is hostility to God, the unfaithfulness of a bride (4:4). God yearns jealously, but gives greater grace: "God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace" (4:5-6). So submit to God, resist the devil, come near, wash, grieve, and be lifted up (4:7-10).

Do not speak against one another: the slanderer sets himself above the law, but there is only one Lawgiver and Judge (4:11-12). To merchants who plan a year's trading, James says: you are a puff of steam. Say instead, "If the Lord wants it, we will live, and we will do this thing or that." Knowing the good and not doing it is sin (4:13-17).
readings: A prophet's call to repent

Read as a whole, 4:1-10 has the shape of a prophet's summons: the charge (wars, envy, unfaithfulness), the call (submit, come near, wash, grieve), and the promise ("he will raise you high"). James speaks to the church as the prophets spoke to Israel.
Practical wisdom
Others read the chapter as wisdom teaching on desire, speech and planning, close to Proverbs: desires cause conflict, slander usurps God's place, and plans must be held loosely before God.

views.H: "Wars" and "murder" may be strong words for quarrels, or a sign of the violence of the years before the Jewish revolt against Rome. The merchants of 4:13 travel from city to city to trade, as Aquila and Priscilla, Jews who had come from Italy, moved to Corinth and worked at their craft (Acts 18:2-3).
views.C: 4:5 cites "the Scripture" for words found nowhere in the Old Testament. Critical scholars discuss whether James quotes a lost writing or paraphrases. The near-identical use of Proverbs 3:34 in 4:6-10 and 1 Peter 5:5-9 (humble yourselves, resist the devil) is one reason some think one letter knew the other, or both drew on a shared pattern of teaching.
views.L: Commands come in a burst of ten imperatives in 4:7-10, the densest in the letter. "Come now" (4:13; 5:1) opens two parallel addresses to the merchants and the rich.
views.J: God's people as an unfaithful wife (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3), God's jealousy (Exodus 20:5; 34:14), the call to return (Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7), the one Lawgiver and Judge (Isaiah 33:22), and the law against slander (Leviticus 19:16) all shape the chapter.
views.T: 4:7 ("Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you") has been a favorite of Christian teaching on spiritual warfare and temptation; 4:15, with Paul's similar words (Acts 18:21; 1 Corinthians 4:19), stands behind the Christian habit of saying "God willing" about plans.

deep.b:
James writes: "Or do you think the Scripture is speaking for no reason?" and then gives words that no book of the Old Testament contains. The Greek, pros phthonon epipothei to pneuma ho katokisen en hemin, has two problems at once.

Who yearns? If God is the subject, the verse says God longs jealously for the spirit he placed in people, that is, he wants his people's whole love, as a husband does (4:4). If "the spirit" is the subject, it says the human spirit God placed in us tends toward envy (4:2, "you envy"), and the next verse answers that God gives greater grace. A third reading takes "the spirit" as the Holy Spirit, who yearns jealously over believers.

Which Scripture? Readers have pointed to God's jealousy in the Torah (Exodus 20:5; 34:14), to a lost writing, or to Proverbs 3:34, quoted in the next verse, taking 4:5b as James' own comment. None is certain, and the Plain gives one reading with the others in the notes.

deep.title: Claude's theory: friendship, Abraham and the adulteresses
deep.b: James calls Abraham "the friend of God" (2:23) and then, two chapters later, says that whoever wants to be "a friend of the world" makes himself God's enemy (4:4). The word "friend" (philos) appears in the letter only in these two places. I suggest James means them to be read together: Abraham's friendship with God was shown when he gave up what he loved most (Isaac) at God's word; the readers' friendship with the world shows when they will not give up anything, even for a hungry brother. The test of friendship is what one is willing to let go. Luke Timothy Johnson has written on the choice between friendship with the world and friendship with God in James, in studies collected as Brother of Jesus, Friend of God (2004), so the link between the two verses may well be made there. The point I add is the test of what one is willing to give up.

echoes: Proverbs 3:34; 1 Peter 5:5-9; Hosea 2:2; Jeremiah 3:20; Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:14; Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7; Psalm 24:4; Luke 6:25; Matthew 23:12; Leviticus 19:16; Isaiah 33:22; Proverbs 27:1; Psalm 39:5; Luke 12:16-21

settings.what: A call to repent: wars within, friendship with the world, and slander
settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: To churches torn by quarrels and envy
settings.why: To trace the church's conflicts to their root in disordered desire, to call the readers back to God with the language of the prophets, and to stop them from judging one another. Knowing they were a poor community envying the rich explains why "friendship with the world" is a live danger: the world's values were the values of the people who oppressed them.
views: "Wars" and "murder" describe church quarrels and hatred in the language of Jesus (Matthew 5:21-22).
Some readers think of actual violence among Jewish groups in the years before AD 66, which members could be drawn into.

settings.what: To the merchants: "If the Lord wills"
settings.to: Traders who plan a year of business in another city, within or near the communities James writes to
settings.why: To puncture the confidence of people who plan profit as though their lives were their own. James does not condemn trade; he condemns leaving God out. The section prepares for the harsher words to the rich landowners in 5:1-6.

title: Patience, Prayer and the Wanderer
sum: In the manner of the prophets, James turns on the rich: their riches have rotted, their gold has rusted, and the rust will testify against them. The wages they cheated the reapers out of cry out to the Lord of Armies, and they have fattened themselves for a day of slaughter, condemning and killing the righteous (5:1-6). The believers, by contrast, are to wait patiently like a farmer for the rain, because the Lord's coming is near and the Judge is at the doors. The prophets and Job are their models, and their yes must be yes (5:7-12).

The letter ends with prayer. The suffering should pray, the cheerful sing. The sick should call the elders of the church to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the Lord's name; the prayer of faith will save the sick, and sins will be forgiven. Believers are to confess their sins to one another and pray for one another, for a righteous person's prayer is powerful, as Elijah's was (5:13-18). The last word is a task: whoever brings back a wanderer saves a soul from death and covers many sins (5:19-20).
readings: Two audiences
5:1-6 is spoken to rich outsiders who will never read it, as the prophets spoke to the nations; 5:7-20 turns to the "brothers", who are told to wait for God's judgment rather than take revenge.
A letter without a farewell

James has no closing greetings. Some see 5:7-20 as a deliberate summary of the letter's themes (endurance, speech, prayer, wisdom, the community) and the final verses as the purpose of the whole: to bring back those who have wandered.

views.H: In Roman Palestine and much of the eastern Mediterranean, large estates were worked by hired laborers paid by the day. The early and late rains, the farmer's patience and the reapers' cries fit that world. Olive oil was used on wounds (Luke 10:34; Isaiah 1:6).
views.C: The prophetic woe of 5:1-6 and the apparent nearness of the Lord's coming (5:8-9) are used in the debate over date: an early setting before the Jewish revolt, or a later one. The anointing by "the elders of the church" assumes a church already led by elders, as in Acts 14:23 and 15:6.
views.L: The letter closes as it opened: endurance (1:3; 5:11), the prophets and Job as examples, prayer and faith (1:5-6; 5:15), wandering (1:16; 5:19), saving souls (1:21; 5:20). There is no farewell, which fits a sermon or a circular letter.
views.J: The law of wages (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15), the prophets' woes on the rich (Isaiah 5:8-9; Amos 4:1), God "compassionate and gracious" (Exodus 34:6), Elijah's prayer (1 Kings 17-18), and covering sins (Proverbs 10:12) are all drawn from Israel's Scripture.
views.T: 5:14-15 is the scriptural foundation for the Catholic sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick and the Orthodox Holy Unction, rejected as a sacrament by the Reformers, and used today, without being counted a sacrament, in Anglican, Methodist, Presbyterian and Pentecostal healing services; see the card. 5:16 has been cited in debates over confession; see the deep dive. 5:12 lies behind the refusal of oaths by some Christian groups.

deep.b:
James' command is mutual: "confess your sins to each other and pray for each other, so that you will be healed." Its setting is the sickbed of 5:14-15, where the elders pray and "if he has done sins, they will be forgiven him." Three readings are found.

Within the sacrament of anointing. The Council of Trent taught that the anointing of 5:14-15 "cleanses away sins, if there be any still to be expiated" (session 14, on extreme unction, chapter 2), and the Catechism quotes James: "if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven" (1520). On this reading the forgiveness James promises comes through the church's ministers.

As support for confession to a priest. Calvin reports that his opponents cited this verse for sacramental confession, and answers that James "joins together mutual confession and mutual prayer. If, then, we are to confess to priests only, we are also to pray for them only" (Institutes 3.4.6). The Orthodox Confession of Dositheus grounds the mystery of penance not in James but in John 20:23 (Decree 15).

As mutual confession among believers. Calvin's own reading: "we are to deposit our infirmities in the breasts of each other, with the view of receiving mutual counsel, sympathy, and comfort" and then pray for one another (Institutes 3.4.6).

Confession of sin to God himself is the theme of 1 John 1:9 and of Psalm 32:5; James' verse is the Bible's plainest call to confess to one another.

deep.h: Anointing the sick: what James describes
deep.b: James' instructions are short and concrete. The sick person calls the elders (plural) of the church; they come to him; they pray over him; they anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. The promise is that "the prayer that comes from faith" (not the oil) will save the sick person, that the Lord will raise him up, and that his sins will be forgiven. Questions the text leaves open have divided the churches: whether the elders are the later order of priests, whether the oil is medicine or a sign, whether the promise is bodily healing, spiritual strength, or both, and whether the rite is a sacrament for all times or tied to the gifts of the first generation. The card below gives each church's answer from its own documents.

echoes: Luke 6:24-25; Matthew 6:19-20; Deuteronomy 24:14-15; Leviticus 19:13; Malachi 3:5; Isaiah 5:9; Jeremiah 12:3; Deuteronomy 11:14; Matthew 24:33; Job 1:21; Job 42:10; Exodus 34:6; Matthew 5:33-37; Mark 6:13; 1 Kings 17:1; 1 Kings 18:1; 1 Kings 18:41-45; Luke 4:25; Proverbs 10:12; 1 Peter 4:8

settings.by: James, speaking like an Old Testament prophet
settings.to: Rich landowners and employers, addressed in the open as the prophets addressed foreign nations, while the letter's hearers are the believers ("brothers", 5:7)
settings.when: To communities whose members worked the fields of such men and were cheated of their pay
settings.why: To assure the oppressed that God hears the cries of the reapers and will judge, so that they need not take judgment into their own hands. If the rich were not in the room, the passage is comfort and warning for the poor, not an appeal to the rich (see the views).
views: The rich are not members of the church: no call to repent, no "brothers".
Rich members may be in view too, as a warning of what they are becoming.

settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: While the readers were suffering under the rich and tempted to grumble against one another
settings.why: To turn anger into patience: the Lord is coming, the Judge is at the doors, and the prophets and Job show that endurance ends in God's compassion. The ban on oaths belongs here too: people under pressure swear to be believed; believers' plain word is to be enough.

settings.what: Prayer, anointing the sick, confession, and bringing back the wanderer
settings.to: The "twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1): Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, or on another reading the whole church as Israel scattered (see the views at 1:1); many of them poor (2:5-6; 5:4), meeting in their own "synagogue" (2:2)
settings.when: In the ordinary life of the community: suffering, joy, illness, sin, and members who drift away
settings.why: To make prayer the community's answer to every situation, to give the sick a way to call on the church's leaders, to join healing with confession and forgiveness, and to send every member after anyone who wanders. The letter ends not with a farewell but with the community's shared work.

traditions.q: James tells the sick to call the elders, who are to pray over them and anoint them with oil, with the promise that the prayer of faith will save the sick and their sins will be forgiven (5:14-15). Is this a sacrament for the church today, and what does it do?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent taught that this anointing "was instituted by Christ our Lord, as truly and properly a sacrament of the new law; insinuated indeed in Mark, but recommended and promulgated to the faithful by James the Apostle, and brother of the Lord" (session 14, chapter 1), and that James' "presbyters" are priests ordained by a bishop (canon 4). The Catechism teaches that it "is not a sacrament for those only who are at the point of death" (1514), that only priests give it (1516), and that it brings strength, peace and the healing of the soul, "but also of the body if such is God's will" (1520).

Yes. Holy Unction is one of the seven mysteries: "the Holy Oil or Prayer-Oil is spoken of in Mark, and is expressly witnessed to by the Lord's brother" (Confession of Dositheus, Decree 15). The Orthodox Church in America teaches that its "express purpose ... is healing and forgiveness", that it is "not reserved for the moment of death", and that the rite calls for seven priests.

Not a sacrament. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531) counts extreme unction among the "rites received from the Fathers" which "do not have God's command" and are not necessary to salvation (Article 13). Lutheran churches differ in practice. The Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod, asked "Why don't Lutherans anoint with oil?", answers that James 5:14 speaks of oil "in the context of receiving medical help", using the Greek word for a medicinal use of oil, and that a ceremonial anointing "is neither commanded nor forbidden in Scripture".

No sacrament. Calvin held that the anointing in Mark and James went with the gift of healing, which "was temporary"; the oil was not the means of cure but a symbol, James meant "common oil", and his elders are the ordinary elders of the church, not priests (Institutes 4.19.18-21). Some Reformed churches now anoint in healing services: the Directory for Worship of the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) says that in a service for wholeness "enacted prayer in the form of the laying on of hands and anointing with oil is appropriate", citing James 5:14, and that healing is "the gift of God through the power of the Holy Spirit", not the result of the skill or faith of those who pray.

Not a sacrament of the Gospel. Extreme unction is one of the "five commonly called Sacraments" that "are not to be counted for Sacraments of the Gospel" (Article 25). The Church of England anoints the sick all the same. Its authorized services for "Wholeness and Healing" in Common Worship include the laying on of hands with prayer and anointing, a prayer over the oil that recalls how "his apostles anointed the sick in your name", and the words "N, I anoint you in the name of God who gives you life. Receive Christ's forgiveness, his healing and his love."

Not a sacrament; anointing is offered in healing services. The British Methodist Worship Book (1999) has "An Order of Service for Healing and Wholeness", in which "the laying on of hands and/or anointing with oil together with prayer for others, as practised by the early Church, may also form part of the service". It lists James 5:13-16 among the readings, applies the oil to the forehead, and blesses it with the words "bless this oil for the healing of the sick".

Not an ordinance. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) names "the two ordinances of Christ" (article 6), baptism and the Lord's Supper (article 7), and says nothing about anointing the sick or about James 5:14.

Not a sacrament but a command to obey. Thomas E. Trask, as General Superintendent of the Assemblies of God, wrote from James 5:14-15 that "we are instructed to lay hands on the sick, anoint them with oil, and pray the prayer of faith", that the minister's task is to "pray for the sick, anoint them with oil, and leave the results in the hands of the Lord", that "No Scripture instructs a minister to tell people they are healed", and that "Divine healing was provided for in the Atonement".
